title: Back to Bethel, On to Hebron
summary: Jacob purges his household of idols, worships at Bethel, receives the covenant blessing as Israel, and buries Deborah, Rachel, and Isaac along the road.
historicalContext: The chapter opens in the wreckage of Shechem, where Simeon and Levi had slaughtered the men of the city and Jacob feared that the surrounding Canaanites would unite to destroy his household (34:25-30). Roughly thirty years earlier he had vowed at Bethel that if God brought him home in peace, the stone pillar would become God’s house (28:20-22). Bethel lay some twenty miles south of Shechem in the central hill country and stood well above it. Household gods, amulets, and earrings worn as charms were common in the second-millennium world, and Rachel had carried off Laban’s teraphim (31:19). From Bethel the family moved south past Ephrath, the later Bethlehem, and the watchtower of Eder toward Hebron, where Isaac still lived. Isaac’s death, recorded at the chapter’s close, took place about twelve years after Joseph was sold, and is placed here to finish the record of Isaac’s generation before the Joseph story begins.
literaryContext: Genesis 35 closes the account of Isaac’s family line that began at 25:19 and brings Jacob’s story full circle. The flight from Esau began at Bethel; the homecoming returns there and ends at his father’s tent in Hebron. The chapter follows Jacob’s itinerary, Shechem, Bethel, Ephrath, Migdal-eder, Hebron, and alternates scenes of grace with notices of grief: purification and an altar, then Deborah’s burial; God’s appearing and blessing, then Rachel’s death; Benjamin’s birth, then Reuben’s sin. The renewed promise in verses 9-13 deliberately echoes God’s words to Abraham in chapter 17, with the same divine title, a changed name, and the promise of kings. The list of twelve sons gathers the births of chapters 29-30 and 35 and prepares for the tribes. Isaac’s death and burial by Esau and Jacob mirror Abraham’s in 25:7-10, and Esau’s genealogy follows in chapter 36, just as Ishmael’s followed Abraham’s death.
themes: Putting away idols before meeting God
God’s protection of a weak and compromised family
The covenant blessing confirmed to Israel
Sorrow and death along the road of faith
The twelve sons as the foundation of the tribes

outline.title: A Household Made Clean
outline.summary: God calls Jacob back to Bethel; the family surrenders its idols and earrings, washes and changes garments, and travels under God’s protection.

outline.title: Worship and Blessing at Bethel
outline.summary: Jacob builds an altar to the God of Bethel, mourns Deborah, and hears God confirm the name Israel and the promises of offspring, kings, and land.

outline.title: Rachel’s Death and Benjamin’s Birth
outline.summary: Near Ephrath Rachel dies giving birth to her second son, names him Ben-oni with her last breath, and is buried beneath a pillar.

outline.title: Reuben’s Sin and the Twelve Sons
outline.summary: Reuben defiles his father’s concubine, and the narrator lists the twelve sons of Jacob by their mothers.

outline.title: Isaac Laid to Rest
outline.summary: Jacob reaches his father at Hebron; Isaac dies at one hundred eighty years and is buried by Esau and Jacob together.

verses.bibleText: And God said unto Jacob, Arise, go up to Beth-el, and dwell there: and make there an altar unto God, that appeared unto thee when thou fleddest from the face of Esau thy brother.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter turns on a fresh word from God. At the end of chapter 34 Jacob was paralysed by fear, sure that the Canaanites would gather and wipe out his household because of what Simeon and Levi had done at Shechem (34:30). He had no plan, and his sons had answered his rebuke with defiance. Into that helplessness God speaks: “Arise, go up to Beth-el, and dwell there.” The initiative belongs entirely to the Lord. Jacob does not first repent and then earn a hearing; God addresses him in his confusion and points him home.

The command recalls unfinished business. When Jacob fled from Esau some three decades before, he vowed at Bethel that if God kept him and brought him back in peace, the stone he had set up would become God’s house (28:20-22). God had kept his side of the vow through Laban’s schemes and Esau’s approach. Jacob, however, had settled at Shechem, bought land, and built an altar there (33:18-20), some twenty miles short of the place he had promised to honour. The call to “go up” is geographical, since Bethel stands higher in the hill country, but it also marks a spiritual ascent away from a compromised life among the Canaanites.

This is the only place in Genesis where God directs a patriarch to build an altar. Elsewhere the patriarchs raise altars of their own accord (12:7; 13:18; 26:25). The altar is to honour the “God, that appeared unto thee when thou fleddest from the face of Esau thy brother.” God identifies himself by Jacob’s lowest moment: alone, guilty, running, with a stone for a pillow. Divine grace met him then, and the same grace calls him now. The God of Bethel had already introduced himself in those terms when he told Jacob to leave Haran (31:13).

The pattern runs through Scripture. When God’s people drift, he recalls them to the place of first love and first promises (Revelation 2:4-5). Return begins with his voice, and it leads to worship at the place of grace.

wordNotes.explanation: Two imperatives stand side by side for urgency. Qum calls for decisive movement, and ‘alah is the ordinary verb for travelling to higher ground; Bethel lies well above Shechem. The same verb is used of going up to worship at a sanctuary (1 Samuel 1:3), and later of pilgrims going up to Jerusalem (Psalm 122:4). Jacob echoes the pair in verse 3 when he summons his family.

“House of God,” the name Jacob gave the place after his dream of the stairway (28:17-19). God’s command takes Jacob back not merely to a town but to the place that stands for the Lord’s first gracious appearance to him. Later Israel would corrupt Bethel with the golden calf, and Hosea mocks it as “Beth-aven,” house of wickedness (1 Kings 12:28-29; Hosea 4:15).

verses.bibleText: Then Jacob said unto his household, and to all that were with him, Put away the strange gods that are among you, and be clean, and change your garments:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob responds at once, and the first thing he addresses is not the journey but the household. “Put away the strange gods that are among you.” He speaks to his family “and to all that were with him,” a wider group that by now included servants and very likely the women and children taken captive from Shechem (34:29). The phrase “among you” admits what had been tolerated. Rachel had stolen her father’s teraphim (31:19), servants from Haran may have brought their own images, and the plunder of Shechem would have carried idols and cultic objects into the camp. Jacob knew they were there. A summons to meet the God of Bethel made their presence impossible to ignore.

Three commands follow, and they move from the heart outward. The first deals with allegiance: the foreign gods must go. The second, “be clean,” calls for purification. The family had been defiled in more than one sense by the events at Shechem, by Dinah’s violation (34:5) and by the slaughter and looting that followed. Later law would require those who had touched the slain to purify themselves and their garments before rejoining the camp (Numbers 31:19-20). The third, “change your garments,” gives outward expression to the inward change.

The sequence closely resembles the preparation God required of Israel before Sinai, where the people washed their clothes and sanctified themselves to meet him (Exodus 19:10-11). Coming into God’s presence is never casual. Holiness is implied even though Genesis rarely uses the word, and Jacob’s instructions show that he grasped it.

The New Testament takes up the same picture. Believers are told to put off the old self with its practices and put on the new, created after God in righteousness (Ephesians 4:22-24; Colossians 3:9-10). Paul applies the call to separation directly: because God dwells among his people, they are to come out from idolatry and cleanse themselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit (2 Corinthians 6:16-7:1). The washing itself did not make Jacob’s household acceptable. Grace had already called them; the washing and the change of clothing expressed a surrender that the heart had to make first. Joshua would later stand at Shechem and issue nearly the same summons to the nation: “put away the strange gods which are among you” (Joshua 24:23).

wordNotes.term: אֱלֹהֵי הַנֵּכָר (’elohei hannekhar) — the strange gods
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “gods of the foreigner,” deities belonging to other peoples. The phrase becomes a fixed expression in calls to covenant renewal, nearly always with the verb “put away” (Joshua 24:23; Judges 10:16; 1 Samuel 7:3). The repeated pairing shows that returning to the Lord always involved removing rivals. Exclusive loyalty is the heart of the first commandment (Exodus 20:3).

A reflexive form of taher, “to be pure,” meaning “purify yourselves.” The verb belongs to the vocabulary of ritual cleanness that later fills Leviticus and Numbers, where washing body and clothes restores a person to the worshipping community (Numbers 8:21). Outward purification signified the inward cleansing that only God provides (Psalm 51:7).

verses.bibleText: And let us arise, and go up to Beth-el; and I will make there an altar unto God, who answered me in the day of my distress, and was with me in the way which I went.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob now speaks as the spiritual head of his household, a role he had largely surrendered at Shechem. “Let us arise, and go up” repeats God’s own verbs from verse 1, but he turns them into a shared undertaking. The whole family is invited to make the pilgrimage, and the leader goes with them.

His reason for going is testimony. God is the one “who answered me in the day of my distress, and was with me in the way which I went.” The day of distress points back to his flight from Esau, when he left home with nothing and lay down alone at Bethel (28:10-15). It may also include the night at the Jabbok, when he prayed in terror before meeting Esau (32:9-12). Either way, Jacob speaks of answered prayer. The God who promised “I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest” (28:15) had done exactly that, and Jacob now confesses it before his children and servants.

The words echo the vow of 28:20, where Jacob set out the conditions under which the Lord would be his God: presence on the way, bread, clothing, and a safe return. Every condition had been met. The only item left outstanding was his own promise. The verse therefore marks a turning point. After years of delay, Jacob publicly acknowledges his debt of gratitude.

The psalmists would make the same confession, calling on the Lord in trouble and finding him a refuge (Psalm 20:1; 46:1). The name “God of Jacob” in those psalms looks back to stories like this one. A father who tells his household how God answered him in distress is giving them the most useful inheritance he has.

wordNotes.term: בְּיוֹם צָרָתִי (beyom tsarati) — in the day of my distress
wordNotes.explanation: Tsarah describes pressure, anguish, a tight place. The noun is used of Joseph’s anguish in the pit as his brothers later remember it (Genesis 42:21) and becomes a frequent word in the Psalms for the troubles from which God delivers (Psalm 86:7). Jacob’s phrase pairs distress with answered prayer, the pattern Jonah also follows when he cries out from the deep (Jonah 2:2).

verses.bibleText: And they gave unto Jacob all the strange gods which were in their hand, and all their earrings which were in their ears; and Jacob hid them under the oak which was by Shechem.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The response is complete. “They gave unto Jacob all the strange gods which were in their hand.” No one bargains to keep a favourite image or a family heirloom. Along with the idols they surrendered “all their earrings which were in their ears.” In the ancient Near East earrings were often more than decoration; many were worn as amulets bearing the symbols of gods and were believed to ward off evil. Israel would later melt down earrings to make the golden calf (Exodus 32:2-4), and Gideon’s collection of golden earrings became a snare to his house (Judges 8:24-27). Jacob’s family seem to have recognized that objects associated with pagan religion and personal display had no place in a household going up to meet God.

That instinct carries a lesson beyond its original setting. The apostles counsel believers to seek the adornment of a meek and quiet spirit rather than outward display (1 Peter 3:3-4; 1 Timothy 2:9-10). The point lies in where the heart rests. Whatever draws attention away from God, or carries the trace of another allegiance, is best laid aside when one comes to worship him.

“Jacob hid them under the oak which was by Shechem.” The verb is not the usual word for burial; it means to conceal. Later reforms burned and ground idols to powder (Deuteronomy 7:25; 2 Kings 23:6), but Jacob’s act was equally final: the objects were left behind, buried at the very place where the family had fallen into compromise. The great tree near Shechem was a landmark. Abraham had camped at the terebinth of Moreh there when he first entered Canaan (12:6), and Joshua would later set up a stone of witness under an oak at Shechem when the nation renewed its covenant (Joshua 24:26). Shechem thus becomes a place where Israel, more than once, made the decision to serve the Lord alone.

A clean break is the wise path with besetting sin. Keeping the old idols as souvenirs invites their return.

wordNotes.explanation: Taman means to conceal by burying, used of Moses hiding the Egyptian in the sand (Exodus 2:12) and of Achan hiding plunder beneath his tent (Joshua 7:21). The ordinary verb for burial, qavar, appears in verses 8, 19, and 29 for Deborah, Rachel, and Isaac. Choosing a different word keeps the idols from receiving anything like an honourable burial; they are simply put out of sight and out of use.

Nezem can denote a nose ring or an earring; here the text specifies “in their ears.” Such rings could be innocent gifts (Genesis 24:47) but were also given for cultic use, as when Aaron gathered them for the calf (Exodus 32:3). Their surrender here, alongside the idols, suggests they carried religious associations in this household.

verses.bibleText: And they journeyed: and the terror of God was upon the cities that were round about them, and they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they journeyed.” The move from Shechem to Bethel took the family through territory where the news of the massacre had surely spread. Jacob had said, “I being few in number, they shall gather themselves together against me, and slay me” (34:30). His fear was reasonable. A clan of shepherds had suddenly become notorious for treachery and violence, and the surrounding cities had every motive for revenge.

Yet “the terror of God was upon the cities that were round about them, and they did not pursue after the sons of Jacob.” God himself restrained the Canaanites. The phrase anticipates the panic God would send ahead of Israel during the conquest, when the nations would melt before them (Exodus 23:27; Joshua 2:9). Here it is protective, a wall around a vulnerable family on pilgrimage.

The protection was pure grace. Simeon and Levi deserved none of it, and the narrator significantly calls the travellers “the sons of Jacob,” the very men whose crime had created the danger. God did not approve their violence; Jacob would condemn it on his deathbed (49:5-7). He shielded them nonetheless because the family carried his promise, and because they were now walking in obedience toward his altar. Had Jacob gone to Bethel in the first place instead of settling at Shechem, he would have had no need to fear. The Lord still guards those who turn back to him (Psalm 34:7).

wordNotes.term: חִתַּת אֱלֹהִים (chittat ’Elohim) — the terror of God
wordNotes.explanation: Chittah, found only here, comes from a root meaning to be shattered or dismayed. The related verb describes people broken with fear (Deuteronomy 1:21; Jeremiah 1:17). Joined with “God,” it may mean a dread that God sent or an overwhelming terror; either way, its source is divine. Exodus 15:16 sings of the same fear falling on Canaan’s inhabitants.

verses.bibleText: So Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, that is, Beth-el, he and all the people that were with him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So Jacob came to Luz … that is, Beth-el.” The narrator gives both names. Luz was the Canaanite town nearby; Bethel was the name Jacob had given the place of his vision (28:19). Mentioning both keeps the history honest and reminds the reader that the site is still “in the land of Canaan.” The promise of the land was real, yet Jacob arrived as a sojourner among its existing inhabitants. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob all lived in the land of promise “as in a strange country” (Hebrews 11:9).

The final phrase, “he and all the people that were with him,” is easily passed over, but it records a remarkable outcome. A family that had been fractured by violence, divided by rivalry, and threatened with destruction arrived together and intact. The God who had protected them on the road brought every one of them to his house. The journey that began in flight thirty years earlier ends in a homecoming of worship, and the circle God promised in 28:15 has closed.

wordNotes.explanation: Luz, perhaps meaning “almond tree,” was the earlier Canaanite name of the town. Judges records how the house of Joseph later captured it and how its name became Bethel, while a man spared from the city built another Luz elsewhere (Judges 1:23-26). Joshua 16:2 distinguishes the two names, suggesting that Jacob’s holy place lay near the town before the name passed to the city.

verses.bibleText: And he built there an altar, and called the place El-beth-el: because there God appeared unto him, when he fled from the face of his brother.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob does what God commanded and what he himself had promised: “he built there an altar.” At Shechem he had raised an altar on land he had purchased, choosing his own place to settle (33:20). Here the altar stands where God directed. Worship offered on God’s terms replaces worship arranged around Jacob’s convenience.

He names the place “El-beth-el,” “the God of Bethel.” Thirty years earlier he named the site for what happened there: it was the house of God. Now he names it for the One who met him there. The emphasis has moved from the sacred place to the Person who made it sacred. Some ancient translations drop the first “El” and read simply “Bethel,” but the longer name fits Jacob’s habit of naming altars after God, as at Shechem (“El-elohe-Israel,” God, the God of Israel), and it matches the title God used for himself in 31:13, “I am the God of Beth-el.”

The reason given is the same as in verse 1: “there God appeared unto him, when he fled from the face of his brother.” Jacob does not forget the shame of his flight. He builds his altar on the memory of grace given to a fugitive. Mature faith does not airbrush its past; it remembers where God found it.

The verb “appeared” in Hebrew is plural, which is unusual with the name of God. It may simply follow the grammatical form of ’Elohim, as happens occasionally (20:13), or it may recall that at Bethel Jacob saw both the Lord and the angels ascending and descending (28:12-13). Jesus later applied that stairway to himself as the link between heaven and earth (John 1:51). The altar at El-beth-el honours the God who first bridged the gap to Jacob.

wordNotes.explanation: “God of the house of God,” or “God of Bethel.” The name shifts attention from the place to its God. The Greek Old Testament and other ancient versions omit the first ’El, but the Hebrew text has it, and the parallel naming of the Shechem altar supports it (Genesis 33:20). God had already called himself by this title when he told Jacob to return home (Genesis 31:13).

From galah, “to uncover, reveal.” In this passive form it means “was revealed,” and the verb is used of God disclosing himself to Samuel (1 Samuel 3:21). The plural form with ’Elohim is uncommon; it may reflect the plural noun or the vision of angels with the Lord at the stairway (Genesis 28:12). The word stresses that the encounter was God’s self-revelation, not Jacob’s discovery.

verses.bibleText: But Deborah Rebekah's nurse died, and she was buried beneath Beth-el under an oak: and the name of it was called Allon-bachuth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Sorrow intrudes immediately on worship. “But Deborah Rebekah’s nurse died.” She had left Haran with Rebekah more than a century earlier when the young bride set out to marry Isaac (24:59), so she must have been very old. How she came to be with Jacob is not stated. Rebekah may have sent her to Haran, perhaps as the promised word that it was time for Jacob to come home (27:45), or she may have joined Jacob after Rebekah’s death. Either way, she had served two generations of the family.

She was buried “beneath Beth-el under an oak,” below the town on the slope, and the tree received the name “Allon-bachuth,” the oak of weeping. Genesis seldom records the death of a servant, and never with a place named in her memory. The grief must have been considerable. Jacob had probably known her from childhood, and her death severed one of his last living links to his mother.

Rebekah’s own death is never recorded. The silence is striking, since the deaths of Sarah, Abraham, Rachel, Isaac, and later Jacob are all narrated. Scripture does not explain the omission, and it is wise not to build too much on it; Leah’s death also passes without notice (49:31). What the text does show is that faithful service in obscurity is remembered by God. Deborah’s name survives where many famous names have vanished (Hebrews 6:10).

The journey to God’s house is framed by graves: Deborah’s at Bethel and Rachel’s on the road beyond. Worship and blessing do not exempt God’s people from the grief of a fallen world.

wordNotes.explanation: “Oak of weeping.” ’Allon denotes a large tree, likely an oak, and bakhut, from bakhah, “to weep,” occurs only here. Genesis often names places after events of grief or joy, as with Abel-mizraim at Jacob’s own burial (Genesis 50:11). Judges 2:1-5 records a later “Bochim,” “weepers,” perhaps near Bethel, where Israel wept under the Lord’s rebuke.

verses.bibleText: And God appeared unto Jacob again, when he came out of Padan-aram, and blessed him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God appeared unto Jacob again.” In verse 1 God spoke; now he appears. The word “again” most naturally recalls the first appearance at Bethel, when Jacob saw the Lord above the stairway (28:13). It may also take in Peniel, where Jacob saw God face to face (32:30), since the name Israel was given there and is confirmed here. Either way, this is a second self-revelation at the same place, framing Jacob’s whole time away. God met him at Bethel going out and meets him at Bethel coming home.

The timing note, “when he came out of Padan-aram,” treats the years since leaving Haran, including the stay at Shechem, as part of the homeward journey. God then “blessed him.” The Hebrew wordplay is telling: on the first visit Jacob was fleeing (barach, v. 7); on this one he is blessed (barakh). The same place that saw him as a runaway now sees him as the heir of the covenant.

Jacob had once grasped at blessing through deceit (27:19-29) and wrestled for it at the Jabbok (32:26). Now it is freely given, with no scheming and no struggle, in the place of obedience. Blessing comes from God’s hand (Proverbs 10:22), and he grants it to those who return to him. Hosea, preaching to Jacob’s faithless descendants centuries later, recalled this encounter: God “found him in Beth-el, and there he spake with us” (Hosea 12:4). What God said to the patriarch at Bethel he meant for the nation too, and the call to return still stood open to them.

wordNotes.explanation: The intensive form of barakh, “to bless,” the key verb of the patriarchal promise from 12:2-3 onward. Jacob had heard this word through Isaac (Genesis 28:3) and at Peniel (Genesis 32:29); here God speaks it directly at Bethel. On his deathbed Jacob recalled this very moment: God Almighty appeared to him at Luz “and blessed me” (Genesis 48:3).

verses.bibleText: And God said unto him, Thy name is Jacob: thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name: and he called his name Israel.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God begins with Jacob’s name. “Thy name is Jacob: thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name.” The change had first been announced at the Jabbok by the mysterious wrestler, whom Jacob recognized as God and whom Hosea identifies as the Angel (32:28-30; Hosea 12:3-5). That Angel, who bears God’s name and blesses with God’s authority, is best understood as the pre-incarnate Christ. At Bethel God himself confirms what was spoken at Peniel, now inside the promised land and before the whole household.

The repetition carries weight. “Jacob” recalled the heel-grabber and supplanter (25:26; 27:36). The name had been justified by the way he lived. “Israel” speaks of one who has striven with God and prevailed, a man who wrestled and clung until he was blessed. Jacob had not become sinless; Shechem had just shown his weakness as a father. But God names him by what grace was making of him, not by what he had been.

The narrator adds, “and he called his name Israel.” God bestows the name, and in this context it becomes his recognized identity. In practice Genesis continues to use both names, often “Jacob” when his weakness is in view and “Israel” when he acts as head of the covenant family (35:21; 46:2). The old nature and the new name coexist in the story, as they do in every believer’s life (Galatians 5:17).

The new name also belongs to a nation. The twelve sons listed later in this chapter will become “the children of Israel.” Paul would later distinguish between physical descent and the true Israel of promise, those who share Jacob’s faith in Christ (Romans 9:6-8; Galatians 6:16). God still renames those he calls (Isaiah 62:2; Revelation 2:17).

wordNotes.explanation: Genesis 32:28 explains the name by the verb sarah, “to strive, contend”: Jacob has striven with God and with men and prevailed. The name is best taken as “he strives with God” or “God strives,” and the narrative supplies its meaning rather than a dictionary root. Hosea retells the wrestling and the meeting at Bethel together, joining Peniel and this chapter (Hosea 12:3-4).

verses.bibleText: And God said unto him, I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee, and kings shall come out of thy loins;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God now names himself: “I am God Almighty.” The title El Shaddai is the one by which he revealed himself to Abraham when he changed Abram’s name and promised kings (17:1). Isaac had invoked it when he sent Jacob away to Haran, praying that El Shaddai would bless him and make him “a multitude of people” (28:3). What Isaac asked, God now grants in person. The title stresses God’s sufficiency to do what human strength cannot, a power that had opened barren wombs throughout the patriarchal story.

“Be fruitful and multiply” repeats the creation blessing given to Adam and renewed to Noah (1:28; 9:1, 7). The words that once applied to all humanity are now focused on the covenant family through whom blessing would reach the world. Jacob already has eleven sons, with a twelfth about to be born, so the command looks beyond his household to the nation that would multiply in Egypt until the land was filled with them (Exodus 1:7).

Three promises follow. “A nation” points to Israel as a people. “A company of nations” widens the horizon. The word for “company” is the term later used for Israel’s assembly gathered for worship, and the Greek Old Testament often renders it with words that lie behind “synagogue” and “church.” God promises Jacob not merely many descendants but a gathered congregation of peoples. The promise to Abraham that he would be “a father of many nations” (17:4-5) is here passed to Jacob, and the New Testament sees it fulfilled as Gentiles are welcomed into Abraham’s family through faith in Christ (Galatians 3:7-9, 29).

“Kings shall come out of thy loins” was spoken to Abraham and Sarah (17:6, 16) but never before to Jacob. The phrase “out of thy loins” will not appear again in this sense until God promises David a son whose throne would last for ever (2 Samuel 7:12-16). Through the line of Judah, one of the sons about to be listed, came David and eventually Jesus, the Son of David and King of kings (Matthew 1:1-2; Revelation 19:16). This is the fullest statement of the promise Jacob ever received, and it came after he had cleansed his house and kept his vow. Obedience did not earn the covenant, which rested on God’s oath to Abraham, but the place of obedience became the place where God spoke most fully.

wordNotes.explanation: The meaning of Shadday is debated; it may relate to a word for mountain or to a root for power. The Greek Old Testament often renders it “the Almighty” or “the All-powerful,” and context consistently links the title to God’s power to give life and fruitfulness (Genesis 17:1; 48:3). God later told Moses that the patriarchs knew him by this name (Exodus 6:3).

wordNotes.term: קְהַל גּוֹיִם (qehal goyim) — a company of nations
wordNotes.explanation: Qahal means an assembly or congregation, the gathered people of God at Sinai and in worship (Deuteronomy 9:10; Psalm 22:22). Joined to goyim, “nations,” it describes a convocation drawn from many peoples. Isaac used a similar phrase when he blessed Jacob (Genesis 28:3). Psalm 22:22 is quoted in Hebrews 2:12 with the Greek word for “church,” showing how the idea of God’s assembly carries forward.

verses.bibleText: And the land which I gave Abraham and Isaac, to thee I will give it, and to thy seed after thee will I give the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The land promise completes the blessing. “The land which I gave Abraham and Isaac, to thee I will give it.” The past tense “gave” is striking, since neither Abraham nor Isaac ever owned more than a burial cave and a few wells (23:17-20; 26:18-22). From God’s perspective the gift was already made; its possession was a matter of time. Abraham had been told the land was his while he walked through it as a stranger (13:14-17), and Isaac received the same promise during famine (26:3).

The promise passes explicitly to Jacob and then to his “seed after thee.” The line of inheritance runs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and on to the twelve tribes. This is the land Jacob had tried to secure by purchase at Shechem (33:19), a transaction that ended in disaster. Here God offers it as a gift. The difference is instructive: God’s promises are received by faith, not secured by human arrangement.

The patriarchs died without seeing the promise fully realized, and Hebrews says they understood that the earthly Canaan pointed beyond itself. They looked for “a better country, that is, an heavenly,” a city whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:9-10, 16). Paul calls Abraham “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and Jesus promised that the meek would inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). The final fulfilment comes in the new earth, where God’s people dwell with him (Revelation 21:1-3). The land promise to Jacob is a down payment on that inheritance.

wordNotes.term: וּלְזַרְעֲךָ אַחֲרֶיךָ (ulezar‘akha ’achareikha) — and to thy seed after thee
wordNotes.explanation: The same formula appears in God’s covenant with Abraham, binding the promise to successive generations (Genesis 17:7-8). It recalls the promised Seed traced from 3:15 through the patriarchs. Paul observes that the promises were spoken to Abraham “and to his seed,” and he identifies that Seed ultimately with Christ, in whom believers become heirs (Galatians 3:16).

verses.bibleText: And God went up from him in the place where he talked with him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God went up from him in the place where he talked with him.” The sentence closes the appearance the way Genesis 17 closes God’s covenant speech to Abraham: “he left off talking with him, and God went up from Abraham” (17:22). The parallel is deliberate. Jacob receives the same kind of encounter, with the same divine title and the same promises, that his grandfather received when Abram became Abraham.

The language of God “going up” implies that he had come down. The encounter was not a dream, as the first visit to Bethel had been (28:12), nor merely an inward impression. Something objective took place at a particular spot, and then the divine presence withdrew. Babel had pictured humans building upward to reach heaven (11:4); Bethel teaches that meeting with God depends on his descending to us. The incarnation is the fullest expression of that pattern, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and the ascension of Christ mirrors this verse on a far larger scale (Acts 1:9).

The repeated phrase “the place where he talked with him” runs through verses 13-15 three times, fixing attention on the spot where God spoke.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּעַל מֵעָלָיו (vayya‘al me‘alav) — and went up from him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb ‘alah, “go up,” marks the end of a theophany here and in Genesis 17:22, where God likewise “went up from Abraham.” Judges 13:20 uses it when the Angel of the LORD ascended in the flame of Manoah’s altar. The wordplay between vayya‘al, “he went up,” and me‘alav, “from upon him,” makes the departure vivid.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he talked with him, even a pillar of stone: and he poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob responds with an act of worship that deliberately echoes his first visit. “Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he talked with him, even a pillar of stone.” Three decades earlier he had turned his stone pillow into a pillar and anointed it (28:18). Whether he now restored that same stone or set up a new one is not said. What matters is the continuity: the man who vowed as a fugitive now stands at the same spot as the bearer of the covenant, and he marks it again.

This time the ceremony is fuller. “He poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon.” A drink offering is a liquid poured out before God as an act of devotion and surrender. This is its first appearance in Scripture; later law would attach drink offerings to the daily burnt offerings and to the festivals (Exodus 29:40-41; Numbers 28:7). Pouring out something valuable signifies that the worshipper gives it wholly to God and keeps none of it back. Paul would use the image of his own life being “poured out” in service (Philippians 2:17; 2 Timothy 4:6).

The oil consecrated the stone, setting it apart as a witness to God’s meeting with Jacob. In Scripture anointing marks people and objects for God’s use: priests, kings, the tabernacle and its furnishings (Exodus 30:26-30; 1 Samuel 16:13). It anticipates the One who would be anointed with the Holy Spirit, the Messiah, whose very title means “Anointed” (Acts 10:38).

Jacob had vowed that this stone would be God’s house and that he would give a tenth of everything God gave him (28:22). The text does not record the tithe being paid here, but the drink offering and the altar show a man keeping faith with his promise. Pillars of this kind were later forbidden in Israel because the Canaanites used them in idolatrous worship (Deuteronomy 16:22). Jacob’s pillar served as a memorial to the Lord, not an object of worship, and it belongs to the period before that prohibition.

wordNotes.explanation: A standing stone set up as a memorial or witness. Jacob raises such stones at Bethel, at Galeed with Laban, and at Rachel’s grave (Genesis 28:18; 31:45; 35:20). The word comes from natsav, “to stand,” the same root used for the stairway “set up” and the Lord who “stood” above it (Genesis 28:12-13). Later law banned the pillars used in Canaanite worship (Deuteronomy 16:22).

From nasakh, “to pour out.” The noun first appears here and later describes the liquid offering that accompanied burnt and grain offerings (Numbers 15:5-10). The poured offering pictured total devotion, an image Paul applies to his readiness to give his life for the churches (2 Timothy 4:6).

verses.bibleText: And Jacob called the name of the place where God spake with him, Beth-el.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob called the name of the place where God spake with him, Beth-el.” He had given the same name on his first visit (28:19). Repeating it confirms that the promise of that night has been fulfilled. The place where a lonely fugitive dreamed of God’s presence has proved to be God’s house indeed, and the vow made there has been honoured.

The naming also mirrors the confirmation of Jacob’s own name in verse 10. Both the man and the place receive their God-given names a second time, now inside the land. The old Canaanite name Luz would persist among the local population for a while (Judges 1:23), but in the family of promise the place would be remembered for what God had done there.

The chapter has stressed three times that this is “the place where God spake with him.” Bethel’s holiness lay in God’s word spoken there. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that true worship depends not on a particular mountain but on spirit and truth (John 4:21-24). Bethel matters because God spoke, and wherever God’s word is received in faith, that place becomes a house of God.

wordNotes.explanation: Maqom, “place,” is a key word at Bethel. In Genesis 28:11 Jacob “lighted upon a certain place,” and the word recurs as the spot becomes holy (Genesis 28:16-17). Here it appears three times in verses 13-15. Deuteronomy later speaks of “the place which the LORD your God shall choose” for his name (Deuteronomy 12:5).

verses.bibleText: And they journeyed from Beth-el; and there was but a little way to come to Ephrath: and Rachel travailed, and she had hard labour.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they journeyed from Beth-el.” The command to “dwell” there (v. 1) did not mean permanent settlement; the same verb can describe a stay of limited length (27:44). Jacob stayed long enough to build the altar and keep his vow, then continued south toward his father at Hebron.

On the road, “there was but a little way to come to Ephrath.” The Hebrew phrase translated “a little way” is a measure of distance whose exact length is no longer known; it may mean “some distance.” Ephrath, identified in verse 19 with Bethlehem, lay about five miles south of the later Jerusalem. The family was still in the hill country of the promised land.

“And Rachel travailed, and she had hard labour.” The verb for “hard” means severe or heavy. Rachel had longed for children for years, crying to Jacob, “Give me children, or else I die” (30:1). When Joseph was born she named him with a prayer: “The LORD shall add to me another son” (30:24). The prayer is now being answered, but at terrible cost. Her early cry proves to be grimly prophetic.

The journey that began with renewed blessing at Bethel carries the family straight into pain. The pain of childbirth is itself part of the sentence pronounced in Eden: “in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children” (3:16). The covenant family is not spared the consequences of the fall, though God’s purpose moves forward even through them.

wordNotes.explanation: Kivrah occurs only in this phrase, here and in Genesis 48:7 and 2 Kings 5:19. It denotes a certain distance of ground, but its precise length was already uncertain to the ancient translators. The context shows that the family was close to Ephrath but had not reached it when Rachel died.

wordNotes.term: וַתְּקַשׁ בְּלִדְתָּהּ (vatteqash belidtah) — and she had hard labour
wordNotes.explanation: Qashah means to be hard, heavy, or severe. The same root describes Pharaoh hardening his heart (Exodus 7:3) and harsh speech (Genesis 42:7). Applied to childbirth, it marks a labour of extreme difficulty, the kind of agony Scripture uses as an image for overwhelming anguish (Isaiah 13:8).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when she was in hard labour, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
In the worst of the labour a midwife speaks. Her presence reminds the reader that Jacob’s household included servants skilled in such work. “Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.” The words are meant as comfort, and they fulfil Rachel’s prayer at Joseph’s birth that God would add another son (30:24). The word “also” links this child to Joseph: Rachel’s prayer has been answered in full.

“Fear not” is the same reassurance God gave Abraham before promising him a son (15:1) and Hagar in the wilderness (21:17). Here a human voice speaks it at the threshold of death. A similar scene occurs at the death of Phinehas’s wife, who was told “Fear not; for thou hast born a son” and died without taking comfort (1 Samuel 4:20). Rachel at least hears that her longing has been granted.

The tragedy lies in the timing. The son she had prayed for arrives as her strength fails. Scripture does not soften this. God’s answers sometimes come in ways that carry sorrow alongside joy, and those who love him still pass through the shadow of death (Psalm 23:4). Yet Rachel’s last conscious moments included the knowledge that God had heard her. A righteous person may find refuge even in dying (Proverbs 14:32).

wordNotes.explanation: An intensive participle of yalad, “to bear,” meaning one who helps others give birth. Midwives appear again at Tamar’s delivery of twins (Genesis 38:28) and as Shiphrah and Puah, who feared God and refused Pharaoh’s order to kill Hebrew boys (Exodus 1:15-17).

The feminine form of a common reassurance. God speaks the masculine form to Abraham before promising a son (Genesis 15:1). The same feminine form is spoken to Hagar and to the dying wife of Phinehas (Genesis 21:17; 1 Samuel 4:20). It marks the moment when news of a child is meant to overcome fear.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Ben-oni: but his father called him Benjamin.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Ben-oni.” The narrator explains his own phrase in the parenthesis: her soul departing means that she died. In Hebrew the word “soul” (nephesh) frequently means life itself, the breath and vitality that make a person a living being (2:7; 9:4-5). When the breath leaves, life ends. The phrase describes Rachel’s life and breath ebbing away as she died, not a conscious being leaving the body to continue elsewhere. Scripture states plainly that at death a person’s breath goes forth and “in that very day his thoughts perish” (Psalm 146:4), and that “the dead know not any thing” (Ecclesiastes 9:5). Elijah later prayed that the child’s nephesh would “come into him again,” and when it did, the boy lived (1 Kings 17:21-22); restoring the soul meant restoring life. Rachel used her last breath to name her son.

The name she chose was Ben-oni, “son of my sorrow” or “son of my trouble.” From her bed of pain, it was an honest name. Rachel had named her other sons, through Bilhah and in her own body, with phrases that reflected her rivalry with Leah and her longing (30:6-8, 24). This last naming expresses grief.

“But his father called him Benjamin.” This is the only son whose name Jacob is recorded as choosing. He refused to let the boy carry his mother’s death as a lifelong label. Benjamin means “son of the right hand.” The right hand in Scripture is the place of strength, favour, and honour (Psalm 110:1; 118:15-16). Because Hebrew orientation faced east, the right hand also meant the south, so the name may also mark Benjamin as the only son born in Canaan, the southern land, after the journey from Aram. Jacob looked past the grief of the moment to the promise. A child born in sorrow would be a son of strength.

The pattern anticipates Christ. Isaiah calls the Messiah “a man of sorrows” (53:3), yet he is exalted to the right hand of God (Hebrews 1:3). In him the son of sorrow and the son of the right hand are one Person.

Rachel rests in the grave until the resurrection morning. Scripture describes the death of God’s people as sleep (Daniel 12:2; John 11:11-14), and her hope, like that of every believer, lies in the day when Christ calls the dead from their graves (John 5:28-29).

wordNotes.term: בְּצֵאת נַפְשָׁהּ (betset nafshah) — as her soul was in departing
wordNotes.explanation: Nephesh means a living being and, very often, life or breath; the KJV translates it “life” in passages such as Genesis 9:5 and Job 2:6. The verb yatsa, “go out,” pictures breath leaving. The narrator immediately glosses the phrase with “for she died.” It describes the end of life, not the flight of a conscious entity. The same expression in reverse appears when the soul “came into” the widow’s son and he revived (1 Kings 17:22).

’Oni most likely means “my sorrow” or “my trouble” (Deuteronomy 26:14), though a similar word can mean strength (Genesis 49:3). Binyamin joins ben, “son,” with yamin, “right hand,” a symbol of power and favour (Exodus 15:6). Yamin can also mean “south” (Psalm 89:12), fitting the only son born in Canaan.

verses.bibleText: And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Beth-lehem.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Beth-lehem.” The statement is brief, as death notices in Genesis usually are. Rachel, the wife Jacob loved and served fourteen years to win (29:18-30), dies young compared with the patriarchs, in childbirth, on the road. She is not laid in the cave of Machpelah with Abraham, Sarah, and later Leah (49:31). She is buried where she fell. Decades later Jacob still recalled the place and the grief: “Rachel died by me in the land of Canaan in the way” (48:7).

There may be a sad echo of Jacob’s own rash words. When Laban searched for his stolen gods, Jacob declared that whoever had them would not live (31:32), not knowing that Rachel had taken them. Scripture does not draw the connection explicitly, and Rachel’s death need not be read as punishment. But the story is honest about the way unexamined words and hidden sin can cast long shadows.

The narrator identifies Ephrath as Bethlehem, “house of bread,” the town later known as the home of Ruth and Boaz and of David (Ruth 1:2; 1 Samuel 17:12). Samuel places Rachel’s tomb at Zelzah “in the border of Benjamin” (1 Samuel 10:2), which suggests a site somewhat north of Bethlehem on the road toward it; “in the way to Ephrath” allows for that.

Bethlehem Ephratah would one day be named as the birthplace of the ruler “whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” (Micah 5:2). Matthew links Rachel to that birth. When Herod slaughtered the infants of Bethlehem, he quoted Jeremiah’s image of Rachel weeping for her children (Jeremiah 31:15; Matthew 2:16-18). Jeremiah’s next lines promise that the children will come again from the land of the enemy (31:16-17). Rachel’s grave on the road to Bethlehem stands near the place where the Son who conquers death would be born.

wordNotes.term: אֶפְרָתָה … בֵּית לָחֶם (’Efratah … Beit Lechem) — Ephrath … Beth-lehem
wordNotes.explanation: Ephrath may be connected with a root for fruitfulness; Beit Lechem means “house of bread.” The two names appear together in Ruth 4:11 and in Micah’s prophecy (Micah 5:2). 1 Chronicles 2:50-51 links Ephratah to the clan of Caleb, whose descendant was called “the father of Beth-lehem,” suggesting how the names became associated.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob set a pillar upon her grave: that is the pillar of Rachel's grave unto this day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob set a pillar upon her grave.” This is the third pillar Jacob has raised, after the stones at Bethel (28:18; 35:14) and the heap of witness with Laban (31:45). The same man who has just set up a pillar to mark God’s appearance now sets up one to mark his wife’s death. The two stones stand within a short distance of each other on the same road: one for God’s faithfulness and one for the sorrow of a fallen world. Both are part of the life of faith.

The narrator adds, “that is the pillar of Rachel’s grave unto this day.” The phrase “unto this day” shows that the monument was still known when Genesis was written. It remained a recognized landmark into Samuel’s time, when Saul was told to pass by Rachel’s sepulchre on his way home (1 Samuel 10:2).

A grave marker in the land of promise was itself a statement of faith. Abraham had bought a burial cave as his first possession in Canaan (23:17-20). Jacob’s pillar claimed no territory, but it declared that his family belonged to this land and would remain. Every grave of God’s people is in some sense a marker awaiting the resurrection, when the earth will give up its dead (Isaiah 26:19).

wordNotes.explanation: A recurring note in Genesis and the historical books that ties a past event to a feature still visible in the writer’s day (Genesis 32:32; Joshua 4:9). It invites the reader to see the monument as a witness that confirms the history. Deuteronomy uses the same expression for Moses’ grave, whose location no one knows (Deuteronomy 34:6).

wordNotes.term: מַצֶּבֶת קְבֻרַת־רָחֵל (matsevet qevurat-Rachel) — the pillar of Rachel’s grave
wordNotes.explanation: The construct chain names the monument by its purpose. Qevurah, “grave” or “burial,” comes from qavar, “to bury,” the verb used for Deborah and Isaac in this chapter (Genesis 35:8, 29). Absalom later raised a pillar for himself because he had no son to keep his name alive (2 Samuel 18:18); Rachel’s was raised by a grieving husband.

verses.bibleText: And Israel journeyed, and spread his tent beyond the tower of Edar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Israel journeyed.” For the first time the narrator uses the new name as the subject of an ordinary journey. The man who had just buried his beloved wife moves on as Israel, the bearer of God’s promise. Grief does not cancel the calling.

He “spread his tent beyond the tower of Edar.” The name means “tower of the flock.” Shepherds built watchtowers in open country to guard their animals from thieves and predators (2 Chronicles 26:10). The site lay somewhere between Bethlehem and Hebron, and its precise location is unknown. Micah later uses the phrase “tower of the flock” in parallel with “the stronghold of the daughter of Zion,” promising that the former dominion would come to her (Micah 4:8). Whether Micah intends the same place is uncertain, but his use of the image within a prophecy that turns immediately to Bethlehem (5:2) is suggestive.

The verse has the feel of a pause, a man pitching his tent and continuing the shepherd’s life of his fathers. Abraham and Isaac lived in tents as sojourners (Hebrews 11:9), and Jacob, after his attempt to settle among the Canaanites at Shechem, returns to that pattern.

wordNotes.explanation: Migdal means tower, and ‘eder means flock or herd (Genesis 29:2-3; Isaiah 40:11). The phrase describes a shepherds’ watchtower. Micah 4:8 addresses “O tower of the flock,” the stronghold of Zion, with a promise of restored kingship, which later tradition linked with the coming of the Messiah near Bethlehem.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when Israel dwelt in that land, that Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine: and Israel heard it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrative now records a grievous sin within the covenant family. “Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine.” Bilhah was Rachel’s maidservant and the mother of Dan and Naphtali (30:3-8). With Rachel only recently buried, Reuben’s act carried more than lust. In the ancient world taking a father’s concubine was a claim to his authority, as Absalom’s public act with David’s concubines and Adonijah’s request for Abishag later show (2 Samuel 16:21-22; 1 Kings 2:13-22). Reuben may also have been acting to keep Rachel’s handmaid from displacing his mother Leah as the leading wife. Whatever his motives, his act was incest under the law later given (Leviticus 18:8), and Paul says that even the pagans regarded such a thing with horror (1 Corinthians 5:1).

“And Israel heard it.” Nothing more is said at this point. The Hebrew manuscripts even mark a break in the middle of the verse, and the Greek translation adds “and it seemed evil in his sight.” The narrator’s silence about Jacob’s reaction recalls his silence after Dinah’s violation (34:5). Jacob’s response comes years later on his deathbed: “Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father’s bed” (49:4). Reuben lost the rights of the firstborn; the double portion passed to Joseph’s sons and the leadership to Judah (1 Chronicles 5:1-2). Sin within the family of promise had real consequences, even though the family itself was not cast off.

The second half of the verse turns abruptly: “Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.” The placement is pointed. Immediately after the firstborn’s sin, the narrator lists all twelve sons, Reuben included. God’s purpose did not depend on the worthiness of Jacob’s sons. Through their failures, and through the long discipline of the Joseph story, God would shape them into the twelve tribes. Reuben himself later showed signs of change, trying to save Joseph from his brothers (37:21-22). Grace does not excuse sin, but it continues to work where sin has done its damage (Romans 5:20).

wordNotes.explanation: A secondary wife of lower legal status than a principal wife, though the relationship was binding. Bilhah had been given to Jacob by Rachel and is also called his wife (Genesis 30:4). Taking a king’s or chief’s concubines was a recognized bid for his position (2 Samuel 3:7-8; 2 Samuel 16:21-22).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל (vayyishma‘ Yisra’el) — and Israel heard it
wordNotes.explanation: Shama‘ means “hear,” and often “take note of” with a view to action, as when God “heard” Miriam and Aaron’s complaint (Numbers 12:2). Here no immediate action follows. The report remains in Jacob’s memory until he pronounces judgment on Reuben in his final words (Genesis 49:3-4).

verses.bibleText: The sons of Leah; Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and Simeon, and Levi, and Judah, and Issachar, and Zebulun:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list of the twelve begins with Leah’s six sons: “Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, and Simeon, and Levi, and Judah, and Issachar, and Zebulun.” The sons are grouped by their mothers rather than by strict order of birth, with the principal wives first. Leah comes first because her sons were born first and because she was Jacob’s first wife (29:31-35; 30:17-20).

The note “Jacob’s firstborn” stands beside Reuben’s name just after his sin. He remains the firstborn by birth, but the honour has been compromised. Simeon and Levi, next in line, had disgraced themselves at Shechem (34:25). The fourth name, Judah, becomes the line of kings (49:10) and of Christ, “the Lion of the tribe of Juda” (Revelation 5:5).

wordNotes.explanation: The firstborn son normally received a double share of the inheritance and family leadership (Deuteronomy 21:17). Reuben is called bekhor here and in Genesis 49:3, yet Chronicles explains that his birthright passed to the sons of Joseph because of his sin (1 Chronicles 5:1).

verses.bibleText: The sons of Rachel; Joseph, and Benjamin:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The sons of Rachel; Joseph, and Benjamin.” The shortest entry carries the weight of the story that follows. Rachel bore only two sons, the first after years of barrenness and the second at the cost of her life. Joseph, already Jacob’s favourite, will dominate the remainder of Genesis, and Benjamin will become the son Jacob refuses to let go (42:4, 38).

The sons of the beloved wife stand second in the list, behind Leah’s. Affection did not alter the order. Through Joseph the family would be preserved in famine (45:7), and from Benjamin’s tribe would come Israel’s first king and, centuries later, the apostle Paul (1 Samuel 9:1-2; Philippians 3:5).

wordNotes.explanation: Rachel explained the name with two verbs: God had “taken away” (’asaf) her reproach, and she prayed that the Lord would “add” (yasaf) another son (Genesis 30:23-24). Benjamin’s birth fulfilled that prayer. Joseph’s name thus already pointed toward his brother.

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid; Dan, and Naphtali:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s handmaid; Dan, and Naphtali.” Rachel had given Bilhah to Jacob during her years of barrenness, and she named both boys with words of vindication and struggle (30:3-8). They are listed immediately after Rachel’s own sons, because legally they counted as hers.

Bilhah’s name stands here only three verses after Reuben’s sin with her. The list treats her sons as full members of Israel. Dan would later receive Jacob’s blessing as a judge of his people (49:16), and Naphtali’s territory in Galilee would see the light of Christ’s ministry (Isaiah 9:1-2; Matthew 4:13-16).

wordNotes.explanation: A female servant, especially one attached to her mistress. Hagar was Sarah’s shifchah (Genesis 16:1), and both Bilhah and Zilpah were given to Jacob’s wives at marriage (Genesis 29:24, 29). A child born to a shifchah on her mistress’s behalf was counted as the mistress’s own (Genesis 30:3).

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Zilpah, Leah's handmaid; Gad, and Asher: these are the sons of Jacob, which were born to him in Padan-aram.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the sons of Zilpah, Leah’s handmaid; Gad, and Asher.” Leah gave Zilpah to Jacob when she stopped bearing for a time, and named these boys with words of good fortune and happiness (30:9-13). Leah’s handmaid closes the list, so that Leah’s family frames those of Rachel and Bilhah.

The summary follows: “these are the sons of Jacob, which were born to him in Padan-aram.” Strictly, Benjamin was born in Canaan, as the chapter has just shown. The narrator speaks of the whole group as the fruit of Jacob’s years away; Benjamin’s birth on the homeward road belongs to the same journey that began when Jacob left for Padan-aram. The point is that the family that went out as one man has come back as twelve sons.

Jacob had left home with nothing but a staff (32:10). He returns with the founders of a nation. The twelve tribes named after these sons will later be inscribed on the gates of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12), and the apostles chosen by Christ will match their number (Matthew 19:28).

wordNotes.explanation: “The plain of Aram,” the region around Haran in upper Mesopotamia where Abraham’s relatives lived. Isaac married from there (Genesis 25:20), and Jacob was sent there to find a wife (Genesis 28:2). Hosea recalls that Jacob “fled into the country of Syria” and served there for a wife (Hosea 12:12).

verses.bibleText: And Jacob came unto Isaac his father unto Mamre, unto the city of Arbah, which is Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac sojourned.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob came unto Isaac his father unto Mamre.” This completes the condition of the vow at Bethel: “so that I come again to my father’s house in peace” (28:21). God had promised to bring him back, and he has. The fugitive who left with his father’s blessing obtained by deceit now returns to his father as the confirmed heir of the covenant.

The place is identified three ways: Mamre, “the city of Arbah,” and “Hebron.” Mamre was where Abraham lived beside the oaks and built an altar (13:18), and where the Lord visited him to promise Isaac’s birth (18:1). Kirjath-arba was the older name of Hebron, the place where Sarah died and where Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah (23:2, 17-19). The layered names connect Jacob’s arrival to the whole history of his family in the land.

The narrator adds that this was “where Abraham and Isaac sojourned.” The verb describes the life of resident aliens. Even at Hebron, after generations, the patriarchs did not own the land around them. Hebrews takes up this point: they confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims, and in that way showed that they sought a country of their own, a heavenly one (Hebrews 11:13-16). Jacob would later tell Pharaoh that his whole life had been a pilgrimage (47:9).

wordNotes.term: קִרְיַת הָאַרְבַּע (Qiryat ha’Arba‘) — the city of Arbah
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “city of Arba,” sometimes explained as “city of four.” Joshua 14:15 says Arba was a great man among the Anakim, and the city became Caleb’s inheritance under its later name Hebron (Joshua 15:13). Genesis 23:2 also gives both names.

The verb gur means to live as a resident alien, without the rights of a native. Abraham described himself as “a stranger and a sojourner” before the Hittites (Genesis 23:4), and God later reminded Israel that the land was his and they were sojourners with him (Leviticus 25:23).

verses.bibleText: And the days of Isaac were an hundred and fourscore years.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the days of Isaac were an hundred and fourscore years.” Isaac lived 180 years, longer than Abraham’s 175 (25:7) and Jacob’s 147 (47:28). The man often seen as the quietest of the patriarchs outlived them both.

The chronology shows that Isaac’s death is recorded here ahead of its time. He was sixty when Jacob was born (25:26), so he died when Jacob was 120. Jacob was 130 when he stood before Pharaoh (47:9), in the second year of the famine, nine years after Joseph’s rise to power at thirty (41:46). Joseph was seventeen when sold (37:2), which places that event when Jacob was about 108. Isaac therefore lived roughly twelve more years after Joseph disappeared and would have shared in Jacob’s grief. The narrator closes Isaac’s story here so that the Joseph narrative can proceed without interruption.

This arrangement is typical of Genesis. Each generation’s account is completed before the next begins, as when Terah’s death is recorded before Abraham’s call is narrated in full (11:32; 12:1-4). Isaac’s long life also stands as evidence that God kept his word to him, giving him life, protection, and descendants through the famine and conflicts of his day (26:3-4, 24).

wordNotes.term: יְמֵי יִצְחָק (yemei Yitschaq) — the days of Isaac
wordNotes.explanation: “Days” is a common Hebrew way of speaking of a lifetime. The same formula introduces the total years of Abraham, Jacob, and others (Genesis 25:7; 47:28). Psalm 90:10 reflects on the shortened span of human days after the patriarchal age.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac gave up the ghost, and died, and was gathered unto his people, being old and full of days: and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The record of Isaac’s death uses the same chain of expressions as Abraham’s (25:8-9). “Isaac gave up the ghost, and died, and was gathered unto his people, being old and full of days.” The first verb means simply that he breathed his last. The older English word “ghost” in the KJV means breath or spirit in the sense of the life-breath God gives (2:7). When that breath returns to God, the body returns to dust (Ecclesiastes 12:7). The phrase describes the end of life, not a conscious soul escaping the body.

“Gathered unto his people” is a Hebrew idiom for dying and being laid to rest among those who had gone before. It is used of Aaron and Moses, who died far from any family tomb (Numbers 20:24; Deuteronomy 32:50), so it does not simply mean being placed in the same grave. Nor does it describe a reunion of conscious souls in another realm. The dead are asleep, without knowledge or activity (Ecclesiastes 9:5, 10; Psalm 146:4). Isaac rests in death, awaiting the resurrection when Christ returns and those who sleep in the dust awake (Daniel 12:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:16).

Jesus drew on that hope when he answered the Sadducees. God calls himself “the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” long after their deaths, and Jesus took this as proof that the dead will rise, because “he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him” (Luke 20:37-38). The covenant relationship is not broken by death; God will raise his sleeping saints to receive the promise. Hebrews places Isaac among those who “died in faith, not having received the promises” (11:13, 20).

“His sons Esau and Jacob buried him.” As Isaac and Ishmael had buried Abraham (25:9), so the two estranged brothers stand together at their father’s grave. The reconciliation of chapter 33 has held. Esau is named first, as the elder, and his genealogy follows in chapter 36. Isaac was laid in the cave of Machpelah with Abraham, Sarah, and Rebekah, where Leah and later Jacob would also be buried (49:31; 50:13).

Isaac’s life had its failures, especially his attempt to bless Esau against God’s word (27:1-4). Yet he died “full of days,” content with the span God gave him, and his last recorded act of faith was to bless his sons concerning things to come (Hebrews 11:20). The God of Isaac remains faithful to his sleeping servant.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּגְוַע (vayyigwa‘) — and gave up the ghost
wordNotes.explanation: Gawa‘ means to expire or breathe one’s last. It describes the death of all flesh in the flood (Genesis 7:21) and Job’s wish that he had died at birth (Job 3:11). Job also uses it of humans generally: man “giveth up the ghost, and where is he?” (Job 14:10). The verb refers to the cessation of breath and life.

wordNotes.term: זָקֵן וּשְׂבַע יָמִים (zaqen usva‘ yamim) — old and full of days
wordNotes.explanation: Zaqen means old, and sava‘ means satisfied or filled, as with food. To be “full of days” is to reach the end of a long life content. The same description is given to David and Job (1 Chronicles 29:28; Job 42:17). Abraham’s death adds “in a good old age” (Genesis 25:8), a phrase not repeated for Isaac.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What promises have you made to God in a hard moment that you have since let slide?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God calls a compromised family back to the place of his first meeting, they put away their idols, and he answers their return by confirming his covenant, while the road beyond Bethel still holds grief that faith must carry to the resurrection.
discussionQuestions: Why does God’s call to worship lead Jacob first to deal with the idols in his own household?
What do washing and changing garments picture, and how does the New Testament use the same language?
How does the blessing of verses 11-12 compare with God’s words to Abraham in Genesis 17?
What does verse 18 teach about what happens at death, and how does this shape Christian hope?
Why might the narrator place Rachel’s death, Reuben’s sin, and Isaac’s burial immediately after the high point at Bethel?
commonMisunderstandings: Rachel’s departing soul is not a conscious spirit leaving her body for another realm; the phrase describes her life and breath ebbing away as she died.
Burying the idols was not a way of storing them for later use; it was a final disposal that removed them from the household for good.
God’s blessing at Bethel does not mean Jacob’s family would be spared sorrow; three deaths and a grievous sin follow in the same chapter.
“Gathered unto his people” does not describe Isaac joining his ancestors in a conscious afterlife; it is a Hebrew way of speaking of death and burial among those who had died before.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the order of the chapter visible: God speaks first, the family repents and worships, God confirms his promises, and the sorrows that follow are met by a faith that names the next generation in hope.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Hear God’s call to go up to Bethel: surrender whatever rivals him in your life, keep the vows you made to him, and trust him through the losses of the road to the morning of the resurrection.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Repentance and renewal: God calls sinners to put away their idols and come to him, cleanses them, and confirms his promises, and those who die in faith rest until the resurrection.
flow: Jacob’s family had drifted into compromise, and its idols were still hidden in the tents.
God called them back to Bethel, the place where he had first shown grace to Jacob.
They gave up their idols, washed, and changed garments, a picture of repentance and the new life Christ gives.
God met them with renewed promises, and Jacob kept his vow.
Death still came, but Scripture calls it a sleep, and God’s people await the resurrection when Christ returns.
simpleIllustrations: A family preparing to receive an honoured guest clears out the clutter and puts on clean clothes; Jacob’s household prepared in the same way to meet God.
A candle that goes out leaves no flame wandering the room; when Rachel’s breath ceased, her life ended until God restores it at the resurrection.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Is there an idol you need to bury today so that you can come back to the God who answered you in your day of distress?
cautions: Do not present the cleansing rites as earning God’s favour; God called Jacob back before the family washed.
Do not use verse 18 to teach that the soul survives death consciously; let the verse explain itself as breath and life departing.
Avoid shaming people over external details while neglecting the heart; the idols were the root issue, and outward changes followed inward surrender.

reflectionQuestions: What strange gods have I allowed to remain in my home because removing them would be awkward?
Have I kept the promises I made to God when I was in trouble?
When God has answered me in my day of distress, do I remember to return and give thanks?
How do I carry grief, and does my hope rest on the resurrection God has promised?
Do I see my own place in the company of nations God promised to gather through Israel’s Seed?
